  This report constructs a quarterly-rebalanced global balanced index fund from local and global equity, bond and commodity indexes, under a mandate that caps bonds at 25%, equities at 75%, commodities at 15%, single assets at 35% and global exposure at 60%. A global bond return index is first built from 10-year yields. Three strategies are compared: minimum variance, maximum Sharpe ratio and a naive equal-weight benchmark. The mandate's bond cap binds at every rebalance and rules out the low-risk end of the efficient frontier, costing about 0.3-0.5 percentage points of expected return at a given level of risk. # Introduction \label{Introduction}

A balanced index fund aims to deliver steady long-term growth by combining equities, bonds and commodities, with the mix set by rules rather than by an active manager. This report constructs such a fund from traded local and global indexes under a mandate with five limits: bonds and credit at most 25%, equities at most 75%, commodities at most 15%, any single asset at most 35%, and global exposure at most 60%. The fund is long-only and rebalanced quarterly, uses at least ten years of data for its covariance and return estimates, and holds no asset with less than five years of returns. Beyond building the fund, the report asks three further questions: what the mandate costs, which of its rules actually shape the portfolio, and whether optimisation beats simple diversification once costs and risk are considered.

# Data and the bond return index

The universe consists of 14 indexes in five groups: local equity (Large Caps, Mid Caps, and the Value and Momentum factor indexes, plus listed property), local bonds (the ALBI and inflation-linked bonds), global equity (MSCI USA, Europe and Emerging Markets), global government bonds (United States and Germany) and commodities (gold and the Bloomberg Commodity Index). All returns are monthly. The euro-area yield series in the data is identical to the German one and is therefore not used. No rand-dollar exchange rate is available, so global assets are measured in US dollars, which effectively treats global exposure as currency-hedged.

For global bonds only yields are provided, so a return index must first be built. Each month, a constant-maturity 10-year par bond is bought, repriced one month later at the new yield with its remaining cash flows, and credited with a month of coupon. Full repricing rather than a duration approximation captures convexity, and the method handles the negative German yields of 2015-2021. Figure \ref{bonds} shows the result: returns were strong while yields fell to 2020 and turned sharply negative as yields rose in 2022, leaving average annual returns of about 2.5% for US and 1.7% for German bonds since 2005, close to their average yields.

```{r bonds, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Ten-year government bond yields (left) and the constructed return indexes (right) \\label{bonds}"}
Plot_Q4_Bonds(Q4_Bond_TRI(Bond_Yields))
```

# Method

At each quarter-end from December 2019, the fund is re-optimised using all monthly data since January 2010, an expanding window that always spans at least ten years. Only assets with at least five years of returns are eligible, so Large and Mid Caps (which start in 2015) become eligible exactly at the first rebalance, Momentum from 2022 and Value from 2023. Because these assets have shorter histories, correlations are estimated pairwise and the covariance matrix is shrunk towards a constant-correlation target (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004), which stabilises the estimate. Historical average returns are notoriously noisy, so they are shrunk halfway towards the cross-sectional average. All mandate limits enter a quadratic programme as linear constraints, and three strategies are compared:

- **Minimum variance**, which uses only the covariance matrix;
- **Maximum Sharpe ratio**, found by tracing the constrained efficient frontier and choosing the portfolio with the highest expected excess return per unit of risk;
- **Naive (equal weight)**, the feasible portfolio closest to equal weights, as a benchmark that requires no estimates at all.

Weights apply from the month after each rebalance and drift with returns until the next one.

# What does the mandate cost?

Figure \ref{frontier} compares the efficient frontier at the latest rebalance with and without the mandate's limits (keeping only the long-only rule). The shaded gap is the cost of the mandate: about 0.3-0.5 percentage points of expected return at the same level of risk, and a fall in the best achievable Sharpe ratio from 0.43 to 0.38. More strikingly, the mandate removes the entire low-risk end of the frontier. Without it, the least risky portfolio has a volatility of under 5%; with it, nothing below about 9% is possible, because capping bonds at 25% and commodities at 15% forces at least 60% into equities. The unconstrained maximum-Sharpe portfolio would hold about 71% in local bonds, so the bond cap is the expensive rule.

```{r frontier, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Efficient frontiers with and without the mandate's constraints \\label{frontier}"}
Plot_Q4_Frontier(Frontier$Mandate, Frontier$Free, Frontier$Points, Frontier$Assets)
```

# Which rules shape the portfolio?

The quadratic programme returns a Lagrange multiplier for every constraint: a positive multiplier (a "shadow price") means the constraint is binding, so relaxing it would improve the objective. Figure \ref{binding} shows which mandate rules bind at each rebalance. The bond cap binds at every rebalance for all three strategies, confirming that the mandate keeps the fund more equity-heavy than an optimiser would choose. The minimum-variance fund also presses against the commodity cap and the 60% global limit throughout, as low-correlation global bonds and commodities are its preferred diversifiers. The maximum-Sharpe fund is pinned at the 35% cap on MSCI USA, the asset with the highest estimated return, which shows that the single-asset cap is what stops it from concentrating in US equities.

```{r binding, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "Binding mandate constraints at each quarterly rebalance \\label{binding}"}
Plot_Q4_Binding(Q4_Binding(Reb))
```

# The portfolios

Figure \ref{weights} shows how each strategy allocates across asset groups over time, and Figure \ref{donuts} the latest allocation. The maximum-Sharpe fund holds 25% local bonds and no global bonds, concentrating its equity in MSCI USA and local large caps. The minimum-variance fund is the most diversified across asset classes, with 20% in global bonds and 15% in commodities alongside its equity. The naive fund stays close to equal weights, adjusted only where the bond and commodity caps require it.

```{r weights, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Asset-group weights at each rebalance \\label{weights}"}
Plot_Q4_Weights(Weights)
```

```{r donuts, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Latest allocation by asset group \\label{donuts}"}
Plot_Q4_Donuts(Weights)
```

# Out-of-sample performance

Table \ref{tab:stats} and Figure \ref{perf} summarise performance from January 2020 to September 2026. The maximum-Sharpe fund earned the highest return (11.8% a year), but with the highest volatility and by far the deepest drawdown (-23% in the COVID-19 crash). The minimum-variance fund earned almost as much (11.1%) with much less risk, giving the best Sharpe ratio and a maximum drawdown of only -14%. Both optimised funds beat the naive benchmark, which earned 9.8% a year. The cost of optimisation is turnover: the optimised funds trade about 5% of the portfolio per quarter on average against under 1% for the naive fund, with large rebalances in 2020 as the COVID-19 shock changed the estimated covariances.

```{r stats, results = "asis"}
Q4_Stats(Port, Cash) %>%
    left_join(Q4_Turnover(Weights) %>% group_by(Strategy) %>% summarise(`Avg. turnover` = mean(Turnover)), by = "Strategy") %>%
    mutate(across(c(`Ann. return`, `Ann. volatility`, `Max drawdown`, `Worst month`, `Avg. turnover`), ~ .x * 100)) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "Out-of-sample performance, January 2020 - September 2026 (returns, volatility, drawdown and quarterly turnover in \\%) \\label{tab:stats}", Digits = 2)
```

```{r perf, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "Growth of R100 and drawdowns \\label{perf}"}
Plot_Q4_Performance(Port)
```

Figure \ref{violins} looks at the shape of the monthly returns. The three funds have similar typical months, but their left tails differ: the minimum-variance fund's returns are close to symmetric (skewness of -0.36), while the maximum-Sharpe and naive funds show long left tails (skewness of -1.27 and -1.09) driven by sharp losses in equity sell-offs.

```{r violins, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Distribution of monthly returns \\label{violins}"}
Plot_Q4_Violins(Port)
```

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

A global balanced index fund can be built from the available indexes within the mandate, and quarterly optimisation adds value over simple equal weighting. The minimum-variance fund is the most attractive: it delivered nearly the highest return with the lowest volatility, the smallest drawdown and the most symmetric return profile, and it relies only on covariance estimates, which are far more reliable than return forecasts. The mandate itself, however, deserves scrutiny. Its 25% bond cap binds at every rebalance, rules out the low-risk part of the efficient frontier and costs about 0.3-0.5 percentage points of expected return at a given level of risk; for a fund described as balanced, a higher bond limit would be worth considering. Two caveats apply: global assets are measured in US dollars because no exchange rate is available, so the rand's effect on returns is not captured, and the out-of-sample period of under seven years includes only one major sell-off.
